the role spelled out in the Constitution itself. That principle was affirmed 
in Bowsher v. Synar, 4:13 U.S. 714 (1986), which invalidated part of the 
Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985 (“Gramm- 
Rudman-Holhngs”). That Act vested the Comptroller General of the United 
States with a significant law execution function even though the 
Comptroller General is removable from office by Joint Resolution, i.e., by 
statute.
Gramm-Rudman-HoUings was an unsuccessful congressional attempt 
to force itself, within five years, to achieve a balanced budget. In somewhat 
oversimplified form, the scheme worked like this: At the start of each fiscal 
year, a calculation would be made about the difference between the federal 
government’s anticipated gross revenue collection and the total amount of 
authorized expenditures. Had the system worked as promised, the 
authorized difference between those two amounts would be reduced year- 
by-year until it hit zero.
A problem with this scheme, however, is that it is impossible to know 
for certain at the start of any fiscal year what the government’s gross 
revenues will actually be. Predictions have to be made based on a variety 
of assumptions about evolving economic conditions. To come up with a 
number. Congress thus authorized the Directors of the Office of 
Management and Budget and of the Congressional Budget Office, 
respectively, to produce separate estimates. They would then make their 
reports to the Comptroller General, who is the head of what was then called 
the General Accounting Office (now, the Government Accountability Office, 
but still “GAO”). The Comptroller General would review the reports and 
forward an independent set of conclusions to the President. In the event 
that the report required reductions in spending to meet the Gramm- 
Rudman-HoUings deficit target, the President would be legally bound to 
follow the Comptroller General’s report. Following Buckley v. Valeo, the 
Court viewed the Comptroller General’s authority to make binding 
determinations as to the spending reductions necessary to meet Congress’s 
target as a law execution function that could be exercised only by an officer 
within the executive branch.
The Comptroller General, however, has generally been regarded as a 
functionary of the legislative branch. Thus the President nominates the 
Comptroller General for a fifteen-year term from a list of three candidates 
provided by the Speaker of the House and the President pro tempore of the 
Senate. Moreover, GAO’s organic statute provides that the Comptroller 
General may be removed by:
